title: HydraSwap Explained: AMM Mechanics, Asset-Oriented Model, and How the Radix DEX Works
excerpt: A deep-dive into how HydraSwap operates as an AMM on Radix DLT, why Radix's asset-oriented model is safer than EVM-based DEXs, and how the swap process works step by step.
content:
Decentralized exchanges have become a cornerstone of the cryptocurrency landscape, offering a way to trade digital assets without relying on a central authority. At their core, DEXs allow users to swap tokens directly from their wallets by interacting with code that lives on a blockchain. This code typically manages liquidity pools, determines prices based on supply and demand, and settles trades atomically. Unlike traditional exchanges that hold custody of user funds, a DEX never takes possession of the assets; instead, it facilitates the exchange while the user retains control of their private keys throughout the process.

## How Automated Market Makers Work

The most common implementation of a DEX today uses an automated market maker, or AMM, model. In an AMM, liquidity providers deposit pairs of tokens into a smart contract, and the contract uses a mathematical formula to set the price of each token relative to the other. When a trader wants to swap one token for another, they interact with the contract, which adjusts the pool balances and returns the appropriate amount of the destination token. The fee generated from each swap is distributed to the liquidity providers as an incentive for supplying capital.

While the AMM concept has been popularized on Ethereum-compatible chains, the underlying blockchain architecture can significantly influence how a DEX functions and what risks it presents. This is where Radix DLT introduces a distinct approach.

## Radix's Asset-Oriented Model vs. EVM Chains

Radix's architecture is asset-oriented, meaning that tokens are treated as native assets of the ledger rather than as balances held inside smart contracts. On an EVM chain, a token is usually a contract that tracks balances for each address, and any interaction with that token requires calling the contract's functions. This design, while flexible, can introduce complexity and potential vulnerabilities, especially when multiple contracts interact in intricate ways.

In contrast, Radix treats tokens as first-class citizens of the network. Transfers of these tokens are handled directly by the ledger's transaction model, which reduces the need for custom contract logic to manage basic token behavior. The asset-oriented model also aims to minimize certain classes of errors, such as reentrancy attacks, that have plagued contract-based token implementations on other platforms.
